WIC / An investigation in seven scenes / 4–6 min

Eligible.
But can you
get the help?

What stands between qualifying for WIC and actually receiving its help?

By Megan Quigley

Follow the evidence ↓

01 / What WIC offers

Food. Support.
A start in life.

WIC is the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children. It helps eligible low-income pregnant and postpartum women, infants, and children under five who have a nutrition-related need.

It provides specific foods, nutrition education, breastfeeding support, and health care referrals. Food packages vary by life stage; they supplement a grocery budget rather than cover every purchase.

The promise is practical: help during pregnancy and the early years. But there is a distance between being eligible, receiving benefits, and getting food home. This story examines that distance.

USDA: what WIC provides ↗

02 / The national gap

The help exists.
Millions don’t receive it.

In an average month in 2023, an estimated 11.83 million people qualified for WIC. 6.63 million participated. That leaves about 5.20 million eligible people outside the program.

This is a reach gap, not a count of denied applications. The figures do not tell us why each person did not participate. And the picture is improving: coverage rose from 53.5% in 2022 to 56.1% in 2023. A large gap and real progress can exist together.

Source & context

USDA estimates eligibility using survey and administrative inputs; participation comes from program data. Exact gap: 11,829,215 − 6,631,309 = 5,197,906. CY2023 was the latest eligibility-and-reach release found in the USDA series during this September 2026 review. Later caseload totals alone do not establish coverage.

USDA national estimates ↗

03 / The age puzzle

Still eligible.
Far less likely to be reached.

WIC can support children until their fifth birthday. Yet it reached 82.3% of eligible infants and just 26.9% of eligible four-year-olds in 2023. Eligibility does not end when infancy does.

These are different age groups measured in the same year—not the same children followed over time. The comparison cannot tell us how many dropped out, never enrolled, or later returned. Children’s food packages and families’ circumstances also change with age. The chart cannot separate those factors from access barriers. It does sharpen the question: what makes support harder to start, keep, or use as children grow?

Source & context

USDA Table 3.1. The published rounded coverage percentages are shown. Eligibility is estimated; these bars are cross-sectional, not longitudinal. The downloadable age data include eligible and participating counts.

USDA estimates by age ↗

04 / The work before the food

Knowing you qualify
is its own hurdle.

In interviews conducted in New Hampshire and Vermont in 2024, one participant thought WIC began only after birth. Another did not know breastfeeding mothers could receive it. A mother who had moved described re-enrollment slipping behind other demands: “I had so many other things to put first.”

The same research complicates a simple story of dysfunction. Most participants described WIC as convenient once connected; one enrolled with a social worker’s help in the hospital. WIC staff described calls and texts to help families stay enrolled. Information and hands-on support can change the experience. These accounts reveal mechanisms, not their national frequency.

Source & context

Interviews took place February–April 2024 in two New England states; study published in 2026. This small qualitative sample is not nationally representative. The quotation and paraphrases are from the participant findings; outreach accounts are from WIC staff. Accounts are not combined into one invented character.

Read the interview study ↗

05 / The checkout test

Two cartons of eggs.
Two different answers.

Enrollment does not remove the work of shopping. Take this California example: an eligible four-year-old has an egg benefit available. Large white eggs can qualify. Brown eggs do not under the state’s April 2026 rules. California cites cost containment; it says shell color does not change nutrition.

Select a carton to see the distinction. This is a rule demonstration, not a reconstructed purchase. In a separate Philadelphia study, caregivers described WIC product restrictions, shopping inconvenience, and stigma. A card can make payment easier while still leaving families to check which food, which size, and what remains on their balance.

Source & context

California’s revised April 2026 FAQ, pages 5–6, excludes brown and specialty eggs, authorizes large eggs, and permits cage-free eggs. This is not a rule for every state. The Philadelphia study interviewed 40 current/former WIC and SNAP caregivers in July–August 2022; its WIC-specific findings concern product variety, shopping, and stigma. Its SNAP recertification findings are not attributed to WIC here. Philadelphia caregiver study ↗

California shopping rules ↗

06 / After enrollment

Issued does not
always mean used.

A Southern California study examined benefit use from 2019 to 2023. For fruit and vegetables, 69.6% of certification periods reached at least 70% redemption. The corresponding figure for eggs was 67.1%. These measure use of an issued food benefit, not whether someone enrolled.

Lower redemption was associated with later program discontinuation. That does not establish cause. Preferences, needs, shopping conditions, and other differences may matter. Nor do these local results measure national waste. Unused benefits alone prove neither that families do not need help nor that an access barrier stopped them.

Source & context

Study of 188,368 Southern California participants, with repeated certification periods. Table 2: produce 254,506 / 365,738 = 69.6%; eggs 244,775 / 364,908 = 67.1%. Discontinuation means no benefit issuance for two months after certification. Continuing eligibility was not established by that outcome. Observational association, not proof that low redemption caused departure.

JAMA Network Open study ↗

07 / Evidence of improvement

Change the process.
More children can take part.

There is evidence that design matters. A national study compared states as WIC moved from paper vouchers to electronic cards. Three years after implementation, participation among children ages one to four was 9.12% higher relative to the comparison. That is a relative increase, not a 9.12-point rise in coverage.

This study does not explain the whole national trend or prove that every access problem has the same fix. It does give us a reason to examine the process, not just the family. The remaining question is concrete: which changes help eligible families receive and use support—and where are they still being missed?

Source & context

Difference-in-differences analysis using state participation data, October 2014–November 2019. Table 2 compares EBT and non-EBT states. Child estimate: +9.12% (95% CI 3.19–15.39). The design strengthens inference but is not a randomized trial; other state changes may contribute. Electronic cards are an evaluated past reform, not a claim that states still universally use paper.
